title: The numinous
hook: Rudolf Otto named the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in (The Idea of the Holy)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carl Sagan, and the star stuff in your own hand. Your line was the cosmos has a way to know itself. Today a scholar names the feeling underneath the awe.
screen: `THE COSMOS HAS A WAY TO KNOW ITSELF.`

segments.voice: A storm rolls in after dark. The power cuts out. Lightning shows the whole street for half a second, then nothing. Some people pull the curtains shut. Others drift to the window, a little scared, and can't stop looking. Back away, come closer, both at once. Rudolf Otto, a scholar of religion, wrote a whole book about that double pull. He thought it sat near the heart of what people mean by holy, and that the old words weren't good enough for it. He needed a new one.
screen: `THE STORM AT THE WINDOW.` → `BACK AWAY, COME CLOSER.` → `A NEW WORD FOR THE HOLY.`

segments.voice: The book is The Idea of the Holy. First, his complaint. When people say holy, Otto noticed, they often just mean perfectly good. That leaves something out: something stranger than goodness, a sense of a presence that is wholly other. So from the Latin numen, a word for divine power or presence, he formed numinous. Second, he said the numinous can't be strictly defined, only pointed at until the listener recognizes it, the way you'd help someone recognize a smell. So he gave it a Latin description: mysterium tremendum et fascinans. Mysterium: a mystery, beyond our grasp. Tremendum: something to tremble before, so overwhelming it makes a person feel small. He called that creature-feeling. Third, the half that's easy to miss: fascinans. For Otto the holy doesn't only frighten. It attracts, and the trembling and the drawing near arrive together. Fourth, an old scene that holds both halves. In Exodus, Moses sees a bush burning that doesn't burn up, and in the King James words he says, "I will now turn aside, and see this great sight." He walks toward it. A moment later, "Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God." Toward, and away. Otto was a Christian theologian, and readers argue about his theology. His word has traveled far beyond his book. A storm, a birth, the sea at night, a silence in a very old room: some moments ask for a bigger word than nice. Numinous is one.
screen: `HOLY MEANS MORE THAN GOOD.` · `POINTED AT, NOT DEFINED.` · `TREMENDUM AND FASCINANS.` · `MOSES TURNS ASIDE, THEN HIDES.` · then, large: `MYSTERIUM TREMENDUM ET FASCINANS.`

segments.voice: Bring back one moment that made you tremble, not from danger alone but from something too big: a storm, a newborn, the ocean after dark, a silence in an old building. Stand in it again, notice whether part of you wanted to step back and part wanted to step closer, and let both be there without explaining the moment. If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.
Numinous. Rudolf Otto's word for the holy as a mystery that makes us tremble and draws us in. Today's word.
Your line: tremble and draw near. The holy, in Otto's telling, does both at once. That's day one thousand twenty-seven.

howItsDone: Students of religion use Rudolf Otto's word numinous for the sense of a holy presence that is both overwhelming and attractive; some people who practice no religion use it for moments in nature or music that feel too large for ordinary words.

chat.says: What's the difference between calling something 'holy' and 'numinous'?
options: Numinous names the part of holy beyond goodness: a mystery that awes and draws you in.
Numinous just means very good, the way people often use the word holy.
Numinous means frightening and nothing more, a thing to keep away from.
chat.meaning: Otto saw holy often used to mean perfectly good. He made numinous for the stranger part: a mystery that makes us tremble and fascinates at once.
